title: Basie's stagecraft compared with Ellington on television
summary: Greene says Basie had been on stage long before the band and his shyness is part of his act.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, I also think, you know, that those experiences also polished Basie.
Because he -- this rubbed off on him. He could see how Sinatra handled himself, and etcetera, and etcetera. Don't you think so?

Well, Basie to me -- my impression of him -- like from way back -- Basie's been on stage for a long time. Way before he had a band, more or less. I think he worked years ago on the stage. And, I think -- he knew about it.
Oh, you do, huh? Is that right? You think he knew?
I think he knew. I think he knew how to handle himself on stage.
Do you, Freddie? Is that right?
But, -- like -- his ways of -- this shyness and all that -- its' part of --
Yeah. Well, as successful as it is, that would be a good explanation, you know.
And, I mean, like, Whitney Balliett was describing it a couple of weeks ago in New York, and talking about, you know, the pointing with the finger and the lifting of the eyebrows.
-- All that -- and it's down so pat. And, it's when you see it on T.V. that you really see how effective that really all is.
And, I notice that you find how most of the public, you know, looks for him to do it, you know.
And, then I can see -- I watch the audience, you know. You can see them when there's a little gesture with his hands --
-- and they're just nudging each other, and they sort of look for it, you know, because they know that that's him.
It may not, you know, attract some people -- they probably think -- look for him to do alot of great gestures, you know.
He don't have to do it, you know (laugh)?
Just like he hits his one note (laugh) -- you know --
That's right. I mean, it's very terrific to be able to get people to buy --
-- get people to call for what is good --
-- what is great. What puts a smile on your face.
Well, in a sense, it's an act -- like -- it's a very underplayed act, isn't it?
I mean where, just like when Duke went on and sort of did all his -- all that stuff he laid on. That was a big act.

We were always very surprised to see that -- like you say -- you think that Basie is being shy, you think that Basie is being a very modest guy, making out he's not equipped and this and that. And, you would be in a position to compare Duke on T.V. and Basie on T.V., and without a doubt, Basie came through like he was being natural and at ease, and you could tell that Duke was not at ease. And yet, Duke was the one that was so smooth and so everything --.
We used to be so -- and saying 'Isn't that extraordinary'.
The Duke often was self-conscious of the camera.
On camera. It wasn't when he was on stage, but when the camera was on him, he was self-conscious.
You can see he's not quite sure of what he's doing with his hands.
